description: Seeking motivated team members to develop an Astronaut Health Monitoring System and integrated NASA OSD research software. Skills in Python, AI/ML, data analysis, web development, biomedical science, aerospace, or physics are welcome. Interest in space research and teamwork is essential. Experience is preferred but not mandatory.
summary:
Developed by the Nobel Foundation for Human Excellence, ASTRO-IMMUNE is an interactive space biology and Astronaut Health Monitoring Platform built with React, TypeScript, Express, SQLite, and Python analytics.

To address the gap between raw aerospace data and practical health insight, the platform unites two systems: a NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) explorer indexing 20 verified flight and radiation studies, and a Dynamic Astronaut Health Monitor. Users enter 10 physiological parameters (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature, respiratory rate, exercise, sleep, mission day, stress/fatigue, and radiation exposure) alongside a 7-question symptom check-in. A transparent, baseline-aware engine cross-verifies vitals with symptoms to calculate estimated risk levels, render interactive charts, model radiation–microgravity synergy (Ψ > 1.15), and export verifiable reports.

By pairing plain-English gene metaphors with strict scientific provenance, ASTRO-IMMUNE makes space medicine accessible to students and researchers alike—supporting deep-space crew preparedness while advancing Earth-side understanding of immune aging, inflammation, and DNA repair.
details:
Here are the project details for ASTRO-IMMUNE by the Nobel Foundation for Human Excellence:

1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

ASTRO-IMMUNE is an integrated space biology exploration and dynamic Astronaut Health Monitoring Platform built around verified NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) datasets and transparent physiological risk modeling.

How it works across its modules:

  1. Dynamic Astronaut Health Monitoring System: Astronauts or users enter 10 physiological and mission parameters (Heart Rate, Systolic/Diastolic Blood Pressure, SpO₂, Body Temperature, Respiratory Rate, Exercise Duration & Inactivity, Sleep Duration & Quality, Mission Duration, Stress/Fatigue, and Cumulative Radiation Exposure in mSv) alongside a 7-question symptom check-in (chest pain, abnormal heartbeat sensation, shortness of breath, dizziness, headache/vision changes, nausea/chills, and muscle weakness).
  2. Transparent Risk & Cross-Check Engine: A deterministic, baseline-aware scoring engine cross-verifies entered vitals against personal baselines and reported symptoms—producing domain scores, an overall health score (0–100), a risk level (Normal, Moderate Risk, High Risk, or Critical Alert), and actionable recommendations. Users can also ingest wearable sensor API packets or upload historical CSV/JSON datasets, visualize dynamic SVG trend charts, persist records in SQLite (with automatic browser-local fallback), and export .txt, .csv, or .json reports.
  3. NASA OSDR & Plain-English Gene Explorer: Indexes verified NASA spaceflight studies (ISS, Space Shuttle, Axiom, SpaceX, and NSRL beamlines), keeps physical absorbed dose (mGy) strictly separate from equivalent dose (mSv), translates 18 immune-related genes(e.g., FOS, CDKN1A/p21, CXCR4) into everyday metaphors with automatic 
     fold-change-to-percentage conversion, and powers an interactive Synergic Engine demonstrating how simultaneous cosmic radiation and microgravity compound cellular suppression.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Accessible to Everyone (Dual-Depth Design): Students and curious readers can understand complex genetics through plain-English metaphors and percentage shifts, while researchers can inspect exact ISA-Tab metadata, sample sizes (n), standard deviations (SD), p-values, and CSV exports.
  • Personalized, Dynamic Self-Monitoring: Rather than relying on static pre-recorded samples, every health assessment, chart, and alert is computed live from the astronaut’s own entered vitals, symptoms, and customizable baselines.
  • Data Integrity & Traceability: Health records carry SHA-256 integrity hashes and explicit source tags (Manual Entry, Wearable Sensor API, Uploaded Dataset, or Simulated Telemetry), while space-biology views link directly to published NASA OSDR accessions and DOIs.
  • Offline-Resilient & Cross-Device Responsive: Responsive layouts adapt across desktop, tablet, and mobile viewports, and a browser-local persistence fallback keeps health check-ins and exports functional even if the backend API is unreachable.

3. What is the intended impact?

  • Democratize Space Biology: Break down scientific jargon so students, educators, and the public can engage directly with NASA’s open space-biology discoveries.
  • Support Astronaut Health & Deep-Space Preparedness: Highlight how radiation, weightlessness, sleep disruption, and inactivity interact during orbital and long-duration missions (such as Artemis lunar missions and Mars transit), including countermeasure evidence like artificial gravity centrifuges (OSD-288).
  • Bridge Space Research to Earth Medicine: Studying accelerated immune aging, T-cell suppression, latent viral reactivation, and DNA repair under spaceflight stress directly illuminates human aging, cancer DNA repair, and inflammatory disorders on Earth.

4. What tools did you use?

  • Frontend Web Application: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide React icons, and custom responsive SVG data visualizations.
  • Backend & Persistence: Node.js (v22), Express, TSX, node:sqlite relational database (with WAL mode and os.tmpdirfallback), Node crypto (SHA-256 integrity hashing), and browser localStorage fallback.
  • Companion Python Data & Analysis Pipeline (astronaut-immune-dashboard): Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, Plotly, SciPy, Matplotlib/Seaborn, Requests, OpenPyXL, and unittest / pytest for NASA OSDR ingestion, statistical verification, and exploratory analysis.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Plain-English Molecular Metaphors: Converts technical gene symbols into intuitive mechanical roles—such as "The Immune Ignition Switch" (FOS), "The Cell Emergency Brake" (CDKN1A), and "The Cellular GPS Antenna" (CXCR4)—bridging bioinformatics and human intuition.
  • Vital-to-Symptom Cross-Verification: Combines quantitative physiological telemetry with qualitative symptom questions (for example, correlating chest pain or dizziness with heart rate, SpO₂, and blood pressure deviations) instead of treating numbers in isolation.
  • Interactive Synergic Threshold Simulator: Turns an aerospace radiobiology equation (
    ) into live mission dials where users can adjust radiation dose, mission duration, and artificial gravity to watch compounded biological strain appear or disappear.
  • Strict Provenance & Unit Discipline: Explicitly separates whatphysical dose occurred (mGy vs mSv) from how biology responded, while tagging every record by whether it came from manual input, sensor API, uploaded file, or simulation.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Clinical Safety & Ethical Boundaries: Clearly distinguishes estimated physiological risk indicators from clinical medical diagnoses, avoiding speculative black-box ML predictions and requiring qualified flight-medical review for alerts.
  • Individual Physiological Baselines & Spaceflight Adaptation: Evaluates vitals relative to each astronaut’s personal resting baseline and mission profile (e.g., LEO/ISS vs. Lunar/Mars radiation budgets) rather than generic one-size-fits-all thresholds.
  • Scientific Accuracy & Unit Separation: Preserves exact NASA OSDR statistics and prevents conflation of physical absorbed radiation (mGy) with biological equivalent dose (mSv), as well as orbital microgravity vs. ground-based clinostat/centrifuge analogs.
  • Reliability, Portability & Device Support: Engineered responsive mobile-to-desktop layouts, one-click .txt/.csv/.json exports, wearable/Bluetooth/API ingestion pathways, and resilient SQLite + localStorage persistence so the platform remains dependable across environments.
